stories.title_idea: How This Graffiti Artist Made $200 Million Painting an Office Wall
stories.payoff_figure: about $200 million (his Facebook shares at the 2012 listing)
stories.odd_means: took shares instead of cash for painting murals
stories.terms: Paid for the murals in cash, about $60,000 by his own account, or the same value in Facebook stock
move: Painted murals across the walls of Facebook's first office
Thought the whole idea of Facebook was pointless and ridiculous
Took the stock anyway
stories.payoff: About $200 million when Facebook listed in 2012: a stake reported at 0.1% to 0.25% of the company
stories.sting: He has said he thought Facebook was pointless and ridiculous on the day he chose its shares over the cash.
stories.who_real: David Choe (living; a public figure as an artist)
stories.note: The How Money Works reel says '4% of the company'; the New York Times figure is 0.1% to 0.25% (CBS), so never say 4%. The $60,000 is his own account of the offer, not a document. $200 million is the New York Times estimate at the listing, assuming he had sold nothing. He was hired by Sean Parker, then Facebook's president.

stories.title_idea: How This Jobless 27-Year-Old Made $17 Million From One Bank Typo
stories.payoff_figure: more than 2 billion yen in one day (about $17 million at the time)
stories.odd_means: bought the shares a bank was selling by mistake
stories.bigger_party: Mizuho Securities and the Tokyo Stock Exchange
stories.terms: A Mizuho trader meant to sell 1 share of a newly listed company, J-Com, for 610,000 yen and typed 610,000 shares at 1 yen each
move: Watched a brand-new share collapse to its daily floor within minutes of opening
Bought 7,100 J-Com shares for 3.44 billion yen
Sold 1,100 of them the same day
Was paid 912,000 yen a share for the other 6,000 when the bad order was settled in cash
stories.payoff: More than 2 billion yen of profit, declared in his own filing to Japan's Ministry of Finance; the typo first cost Mizuho about 27 billion yen
stories.sting: The bank had offered 42 times more shares than the company had in existence.
stories.who_real: Takashi Kotegawa, known online as BNF (living private person)
stories.note: His profit figure rests on one wire report (Bloomberg, carried by the Globe and Mail) citing his ministry filing; the error itself is in Mizuho's own notice. The dollar figure is my conversion at the rate Al Jazeera used that week (27 billion yen = $224 million). Arguable angle: he broke no rule, he bought what was offered.

stories.title_idea: How This Man Turned a $2,000 Retirement Account Into $5 Billion (Tax Free)
stories.hook_label: this man, a founder of PayPal
stories.odd_means: put founder's shares priced at a tenth of a cent into a retirement account meant for the middle class
stories.terms: A Roth retirement account took at most $2,000 a year in 1999, and whatever grows inside it is never taxed
move: Opened a Roth account
Bought 1.7 million shares of his own unlisted company inside it at $0.001 each: $1,700
Kept the proceeds inside the account when eBay bought PayPal in 2002
Kept investing from inside it
stories.payoff: $28.5 million by the end of 2002 and $5 billion by 2019, on which no tax is due if he waits until he is 59 and a half
stories.sting: It was legal: the rule caps what you pay in, not what it grows to, and the shares went in at a tenth of a cent each.
stories.note: All figures are ProPublica's (June 2021, from leaked tax records); the other outlets report ProPublica. He has not disputed them. The closest match to the 'completely legally and completely tax free' winner.

stories.title_idea: How This Student Forgot a $27 Purchase That Bought Him a Flat
stories.odd_means: bought bitcoin for a thesis on encryption and forgot he had it
stories.terms: 150 Norwegian kroner, about $27, bought 5,000 bitcoins
move: Bought 5,000 bitcoins for 150 kroner while writing a thesis on encryption
Forgot about them for four years
Saw bitcoin in the news in April 2013
Got back into his old wallet
stories.payoff: About 5 million kroner, roughly $886,000: some 33,000 times his money in four years
stories.sting: He sold only a fifth of them, enough to buy a flat in Oslo, and kept the other 4,000.
stories.note: The 150 kroner is given as $24 to $27 depending on the exchange rate; $27 is the commonest. One outlet says 5,600 coins bought in January 2010; the rest say 5,000 in 2009. Do not state what 4,000 coins are worth today unless the price is read on the day.

stories.title_idea: How This Man in a Basement Turned $53,000 Into $48 Million
stories.payoff_figure: about $48 million at the peak, from $53,000
stories.odd_means: bought a video-game shop's shares that the big funds were betting against, and posted his account online
stories.bigger_party: the hedge funds betting against GameStop (Melvin Capital needed a $2.75 billion rescue)
stories.terms: One $53,000 position in GameStop, opened in 2019
move: Put $53,000 into GameStop
Posted screenshots of the account on Reddit
Talked the trade through on YouTube from his basement
Held on while the price exploded in January 2021
stories.payoff: His posted account showed nearly $48 million at the peak: about 900 times the stake
stories.sting: He did not sell at the top: the account then fell almost $19 million, 39%, and he posted that too.
stories.note: The $48 million comes from his own screenshots, which the New York Times said it could not verify: say 'his account showed'. The stake is $53,000 in most reports, $50,000 or $54,000 in a few.

stories.title_idea: How Two Brothers Made $800 Million From a Team That Does Not Exist
stories.hook_label: two brothers who owned a basketball team
stories.payoff_figure: about $800 million: some $300 million over 37 years, then a reported $500 million in 2014
stories.odd_means: agreed to shut their team down in return for a slice of TV money, for ever
stories.terms: The NBA took four teams from a rival league and paid the others to fold: Kentucky took $3.3 million, the brothers asked for one-seventh of the four teams' TV money 'in perpetuity'
move: Turned down a plain cash buyout
Signed for one-seventh of four teams' TV income with no end date
Folded the Spirits of St. Louis
Cashed a cheque every year as the TV deals grew
stories.payoff: About $300 million by 2014, some $19 million of it in that one season, for a team that last played in 1976
stories.sting: The NBA spent years trying to get out of the deal and in 2014 paid a reported $500 million up front to end most of it.
stories.who_real: Ozzie and Daniel Silna (Ozzie has since died; check before naming either)
stories.note: Not a share or market story (a contract). The $500 million is the New York Times's figure, reported by ESPN; the NBA never confirmed the terms, so say 'a reported'. A 2012 radio piece puts the running total at $255 million.

stories.title_idea: How This Janitor Quietly Built an $8 Million Stock Portfolio
stories.hook_label: a petrol-pump attendant who became a shop janitor
stories.odd_means: bought ordinary shares on a small wage and kept the paper certificates in a bank box
stories.terms: About 25 years' wages as a petrol-station attendant and mechanic, then a part-time janitor's pay at a J.C. Penney shop
move: Read the Wall Street Journal every day
Bought shares in well-known companies
Stored the paper certificates in a safe deposit box
Almost never sold
stories.payoff: An estate of about $8 million, most of it shares: the certificates made a pile five inches high
stories.sting: He left $4.8 million to the local hospital and $1.2 million to the library, the biggest gifts either had ever had.
stories.note: The fortune became known when his will was read in 2015: keep the reel on the shares and the gifts, not on the death.

stories.title_idea: How a Retired Couple Used Lottery Small Print to Make $7 Million
stories.hook_label: a retired couple who had run a corner shop
stories.payoff_figure: $7.75 million profit before tax, on about $26 million of winning tickets
stories.odd_means: did the sums on a lottery's small print and bought tickets by the hundred thousand
stories.bigger_party: the state lotteries of Michigan and Massachusetts
stories.terms: When nobody won the jackpot it 'rolled down' into the smaller prizes, so in those weeks a ticket was worth more than it cost
move: Read the game's leaflet and saw the flaw in about three minutes
Lost $50 on a first $2,200 test
Set up a company and sold $500 shares in it to family and friends
Drove to Massachusetts and printed more than 300,000 tickets at two small shops each time the jackpot rolled down
stories.payoff: About $26 million in winning tickets over nine years, $7.75 million of it profit before tax
stories.sting: The state investigated and found the game had harmed no one: it had brought Massachusetts nearly $120 million.
stories.note: A lottery, not a market, though the vehicle was a company selling $500 shares. CBS says 'over $26 million', HuffPost 'nearly $27 million': use 26. The same report found big bettors bent the rules on running ticket terminals while the lottery looked away; nothing illegal was found.

stories.title_idea: How This College Roommate Collected $229 Million on a Spoken Promise
stories.odd_means: held his friend to a promise made long before the company was worth anything
stories.year_and_place: promise made in the early 2000s, paid in May 2015, California
stories.terms: The founder promised his roommate, the company's first employee, 10% of whatever he ever got from selling his own shares
move: Joined his roommate's camera start-up as employee number one
Was given more than 6 million share options in 2011 to honour the promise
Paid $3.6 million to exercise them in May 2015
stories.payoff: To cover it the founder handed 4.7 million of his own shares back to the company: $229 million at that day's price
stories.sting: It was only ever a spoken agreement between friends until it had to be written into GoPro's filing with the regulator before the listing.
stories.who_real: Neil Dana (living private person); the founder is Nick Woodman
stories.note: $229 million is Bloomberg's valuation of the 4.7 million shares at the close that Monday. What he kept after selling is not public.

stories.title_idea: How This Secretary Copied Her Boss's Share Orders Into a $9 Million Fortune
stories.odd_means: bought whatever shares her bosses bought, in smaller amounts
stories.bigger_party: the Wall Street lawyers she worked for
stories.year_and_place: 67 years at one law firm, to 2016, New York City
stories.terms: A secretary's pay at one law firm for 67 years, in the days when secretaries placed the lawyers' own share orders
move: Placed her boss's order to buy a share
Then bought the same share for herself, in a smaller amount
Told no one
Stayed at the same firm for 67 years
stories.payoff: More than $9 million, found only when her niece went through her accounts
stories.sting: She left $8.2 million of it to send poor students to college, $6.24 million to one neighbourhood charity alone.
stories.note: The copying is her niece's account (New York Times, 6 May 2018). Some commentators ask whether copying a lawyer's trades was proper; nothing was ever alleged against her. That question is the arguable angle, so state the fact and no more.

stories.title_idea: How This Student Beat a Giant Publisher With Cheap Textbooks and eBay
stories.payoff_figure: about $900,000 in sales, around $100,000 of it profit
stories.odd_means: had his family post him the cheap Asian editions of American textbooks and sold them online
stories.year_and_place: sued in New York in 2008, won at the US Supreme Court on 19 March 2013
stories.terms: The same textbook cost far less in Asia than in America
move: Asked relatives and friends in Thailand to buy the cheap editions
Had them posted to him in the United States
Sold more than 600 copies on sites such as eBay
Paid his relatives back and kept the difference
stories.payoff: Court papers put his sales at about $900,000 and his profit at some $100,000
stories.sting: The publisher sued and a jury told him to pay $600,000, so he took it to the Supreme Court and won, six votes to three.
stories.note: A price gap between two markets, exploited legally: the court held that a lawfully made book may be resold wherever it was printed. Never say the books were pirated or fake.

stories.title_idea: How This Doctor Made $100 Million Betting Against the Housing Market
stories.hook_label: a doctor who taught himself investing
stories.payoff_figure: $100 million for himself, and more than $700 million for his investors
stories.odd_means: read the mortgage paperwork nobody read and asked the banks to sell him insurance against it
stories.terms: Insurance on mortgage bonds: he paid a premium every year and collected if the home loans went bad; the first deal, $60 million of cover from Deutsche Bank, was on 19 May 2005
move: Read the loan-by-loan paperwork of mortgage bonds
Got the banks to write him insurance on the worst of them
Paid the premiums for two years while the bet looked wrong
Stopped his own investors taking their money out until it paid
stories.payoff: About $100 million for him and more than $700 million for the investors who stayed: the fund made 489% after fees from 2000 to mid-2008
stories.sting: His own investors had demanded their money back just before it worked, and he had to lock it in to keep the trade alive.
stories.note: The profit figures come from Michael Lewis's book The Big Short (2010) and are repeated by the rest; one summary gives $725 million for investors, so 'more than $700 million' is the safe wording.

stories.title_idea: How This Man Used 12,150 Cups of Pudding to Fly Free for Life
stories.odd_means: bought 12,150 cups of chocolate pudding
stories.bigger_party: the food brand Healthy Choice and the airlines
stories.terms: 500 air miles for every 10 barcodes posted in, doubled for early entries; he found single cups of pudding, each with its own barcode, in a discount chain
move: Found the pudding in a chain of discount shops
Drove round ten of them buying every case: 12,150 cups for $3,140
Had Salvation Army volunteers cut off the barcodes in return for the pudding
Posted the barcodes in
stories.payoff: 1.25 million miles, over a million of them in one American Airlines account: top-tier status for life
stories.sting: He still earns miles five times faster than he can spend them.
stories.note: A price loophole, not a share story. Totals differ slightly (1,215,000 to 1,253,000 miles; the $3,140 covered some other products too). Often repeated but NOT verified here: 25 cents a cup, an $815 tax deduction for the gift, the Y2K excuse. Leave those out or source them.

stories.title_idea: How This Man Bought a Football Club for 1 Pound and Sold It for Millions
stories.payoff_figure: about £17 million for a club that cost him £1
stories.odd_means: bought a broke football club for a pound, debts and all
stories.bigger_party: the billionaire he sold it to, Roman Abramovich
stories.terms: £1 for Chelsea Football Club in 1982, plus debts of about £1.5 million
move: Paid £1 for a club in the second division
Took on its debts
Ran it for 21 years
Sold it to a Russian billionaire in 2003 in a deal worth £140 million
stories.payoff: His own shares brought him about £17 million from a deal that valued the club at £140 million
stories.sting: He sold too early: the man he sold it to sold the club in 2022 for £2.5 billion.
stories.who_real: Ken Bates (died July 2026, aged 94; public figure)
stories.note: His personal take is given as £17 million or £18 million (Wikipedia has both): say 'about £17 million'. Debts taken on are £1.5 million in most sources, £2 million in one. The 2022 figure is £2.5 billion for the club, £4.25 billion with promised investment.

stories.title_idea: How a High School Turned $15,000 Into $24 Million on One App
stories.odd_means: put school money into an app a parent's children would not put down
stories.bigger_party: the venture capitalists who came in later and paid more
stories.terms: $15,000 from the school's fund in Snapchat's first funding round in 2012
move: A parent who invested for a living saw his children glued to a new app
He invested and asked the school to put in $15,000 beside him
The school held for five years
It sold 1.4 million shares at the $17 listing price in March 2017
stories.payoff: About $24 million for two-thirds of its shares: some 1,600 times the stake
stories.sting: It kept the other third, and the shares closed their first day at $24.48.
stories.who_real: Saint Francis High School, Mountain View; the parent was Barry Eggers of Lightspeed Venture Partners
stories.note: A small institution, not a person: lead with the parent or 'a school'. The school never gave its own total; $24 million is 1.4 million shares at $17. One headline said $50 million (ignore it).

stories.title_idea: How This Couple Turned Their Savings Into a Possible $30 Billion
stories.hook_label: a couple who backed their son's online bookshop
stories.payoff_figure: up to $30 billion (Bloomberg's best-case estimate in 2018)
stories.odd_means: put their savings into their son's start-up after he told them they would probably lose it
stories.bigger_party: the professional investors who came later
stories.terms: $245,573 in 1995, with a warning from their son that there was a 70% chance they would never see it again
move: Listened to their son's plan to sell books on the internet
Put in $245,573 anyway
Kept the shares through the 1997 listing
stories.payoff: If they kept every share the stake was worth as much as $30 billion in 2018: a return of about 12,000,000%
stories.sting: Nobody outside the family knows how much they kept: their holding was last made public at the end of the 1990s.
stories.who_real: Jackie and Mike Bezos (Jackie Bezos died in 2025)
stories.note: An estimate, not a known fortune: always 'could be worth'. The $245,573 is from Amazon's own 1997 prospectus. They gave shares away to their foundation over the years.

stories.title_idea: How This Warehouse Worker Carried Bonds by Train and Became China's First Millionaire Investor
stories.hook_label: a factory warehouse worker from Shanghai
stories.payoff_figure: 1 million yuan in 1988 (about $156,000 at the rate one obituary used)
stories.odd_means: carried government bonds from city to city to sell where the price was higher
stories.bigger_party: China's state banks, which were not allowed to do it
stories.terms: From 21 April 1988 seven cities let people trade government bonds, and the same bond had a different price in each; his first afternoon made 800 yuan, about a year's wages
move: Quit his factory job
Bought bonds the first morning the Shanghai market opened and sold them that afternoon
Read the newspapers in the Shanghai Library to find each city's price
Bought bonds in Hefei and sold them in Shanghai the same day
Asked the police to guard him and his boxes of cash
stories.payoff: His first million yuan, which gave him the nickname he kept for life: Yang Million
stories.sting: Afraid of being taken for a tax dodger, he walked into the tax office in 1989 to ask whether he owed anything.
stories.note: One account ties the nickname to shares he bought in the early 1990s; the bond million of 1988 is the commoner version. A million yuan was a vast sum in 1988 China, far more than the dollar figure suggests.

stories.title_idea: How a Writer and a Mathematician Outsmarted the French Government's Lottery
stories.hook_label: a writer and a mathematician at a dinner party
stories.payoff_figure: about 500,000 livres for the writer alone
stories.odd_means: bought the cheapest government bonds only for the lottery tickets that came with them
stories.terms: To prop up its bonds France ran a monthly lottery for bondholders only: a ticket cost one-thousandth of your bond's value, but every ticket had the same chance of the same prize
move: Worked out that the smallest bonds gave the cheapest tickets
Formed a syndicate and bought up the small bonds
Bought the tickets month after month through a handful of notaries
Collected the prize again and again
stories.payoff: The writer's share came to roughly half a million livres: enough never to need a rich patron again
stories.sting: The government took them to court and lost: they had broken no law, so they kept the money and the lottery was shut.
stories.who_real: Voltaire and Charles Marie de La Condamine (historical; may be named)
stories.note: Figures vary: 500,000 livres is the usual sum for Voltaire's share; one account gives 7.5 million for the whole syndicate. Smithsonian's headline says 'scammer' but the accounts agree nothing illegal was done.

stories.title_idea: How These Twins Lost to Facebook and Became Billionaires Anyway
stories.payoff_figure: a bitcoin holding reported at over $1 billion in December 2017, bought for $11 million
stories.odd_means: took shares instead of cash in a lawsuit settlement, then put the winnings into bitcoin
stories.terms: A $65 million settlement: $20 million in cash and $45 million in Facebook shares, though their lawyers urged them to take it all in cash
move: Sued over who had the idea for Facebook
Insisted on being paid mostly in Facebook shares
Put $11 million of the proceeds into bitcoin in 2013 at about $120 a coin
Held
stories.payoff: By December 2017 the bitcoin alone was reported to be worth more than $1 billion
stories.sting: Before that, the $45 million of Facebook shares had already grown to a reported $200 million by the 2012 listing.
stories.note: 'Billionaires' was a press estimate that depends on the day's bitcoin price; one outlet had to correct an earlier, premature claim. Entry price is $120 a coin in most reports, about $100 in one.

stories.title_idea: How This 10-Year-Old Beat Wall Street With a $60 Present
stories.odd_means: was given ten shares of a video-game shop as a present, framed
stories.bigger_party: the hedge funds betting against GameStop
stories.year_and_place: December 2019 to January 2021, San Antonio, Texas
stories.terms: Ten GameStop shares, bought by his mother for about $60
move: Unwrapped a framed share certificate
Kept it for 13 months
Was asked by his mother: stay or sell?
Sold
stories.payoff: Nearly $3,200: more than 50 times the gift
stories.sting: He put $2,200 into savings and kept $1,000 to invest again.
stories.who_real: Jaydyn Carr, a child (his mother is Nina Carr)
stories.note: A child: a label only, never the name or a likeness. The gift was for Kwanzaa. CNN says $2,000 went to savings, the Associated Press $2,200.

stories.title_idea: How This Man Bought Every Stock Under $1 and Quadrupled His Money
stories.odd_means: told his broker to buy 100 shares of every company selling for a dollar or less
stories.bigger_party: a stock market in a panic
stories.terms: $10,000, borrowed, as war broke out in Europe
move: Borrowed $10,000
Ordered 100 shares of every stock priced at $1 or under
Ended up owning 104 companies
Held for about four years
stories.payoff: About $40,000 when he sold: four times the loan
stories.sting: Thirty-four of the companies were already bankrupt when he bought them, and only four ended up worthless.
stories.note: Details vary: 34 or 37 in bankruptcy, a loan of $10,000 or $10,400, lent by his old boss or 'a friend'.

stories.title_idea: How This Man Made $1 Billion in a Day Betting Against the Pound
stories.odd_means: sold pounds he had borrowed, betting the government could not hold its own currency up
stories.bigger_party: the Bank of England and the British government
stories.terms: Britain had promised to keep the pound above a fixed rate against the German mark and was spending its reserves to do it
move: Built a bet against the pound worth almost $10 billion
Watched the government raise interest rates twice in one day to stop the selling
Kept selling
Bought the pounds back cheaper after Britain gave up that evening
stories.payoff: About $1 billion of profit, while defending the pound cost the British Treasury an estimated £3.3 billion
stories.sting: He was one seller among many, but he has been 'the man who broke the Bank of England' ever since.
stories.note: The profit is an estimate: $1 billion in most accounts, $1.5 billion in some. The lower one is used.

stories.title_idea: How a Welding-Supply Boss Turned $10,600 Into a Billion
stories.hook_label: the owner of a family welding-supply business in Kansas
stories.odd_means: spent the firm's spare cash on 40 shares of one company and kept buying
stories.bigger_party: the bigger rivals squeezing his business
stories.terms: 40 shares of Berkshire Hathaway at $265 each: $10,600
move: Watched competitors move in on the family business
Put $10,600 of its cash into 40 Berkshire Hathaway shares
Bought more within weeks
Held for decades
stories.payoff: The holding grew to 5,800 of the top-priced shares: a fortune of at least $1.1 billion by 2013
stories.sting: At one point he held more of those shares than Bill Gates.
stories.note: Net worth: at least $1.1 billion (Bloomberg, 2013); later articles citing Forbes say $2.5 billion to $2.8 billion. He later sold 1,500 of the 5,800 shares.

stories.title_idea: How One Trader Made $100 Million From the 1929 Crash and Lost It
stories.odd_means: bet on prices falling and hid the size of the bet behind more than 100 brokers
stories.terms: By the spring of 1929 the bet was losing him more than $6 million on paper
move: Sold shares he did not own, betting they would fall
Spread the orders over more than 100 brokers so nobody saw the size of it
Sat on a paper loss of over $6 million
Held until the market broke in October
stories.payoff: Roughly $100 million when Wall Street crashed and almost everyone else was wiped out
stories.sting: Five years later he was bankrupt, with $84,000 to his name against debts of $2.5 million.
stories.note: The $100 million is the biographers' figure, not an audited one. End on the 1934 bankruptcy; do not use how he died.

stories.title_idea: How This Secretary Turned Three Shares Into $7 Million
stories.odd_means: bought three shares of the company she worked for and never sold one
stories.bigger_party: everyone who traded in and out for 75 years
stories.terms: Three shares of Abbott at $60 each: $180
move: Bought three shares in 1935
Put every dividend back into more shares
Sat through every share split for 75 years
Went on living in a small cottage
stories.payoff: About $7 million by 2010, after 43 years as a secretary at the same company
stories.sting: Nobody knew until she left it all to her old college, the biggest gift it had ever had.
stories.note: Same shape as the janitor; do not run the two close together.

stories.title_idea: How a Part-Time Masseuse Became a Millionaire by Asking for Share Options
stories.payoff_figure: millions: she says 'multi-millionaire' and will not give the number
stories.odd_means: asked for share options on top of $450 a week
stories.terms: $450 a week, part-time, with options in a 40-person start-up that she thought might never be worth a penny
move: Answered an advert for an in-house masseuse
Took the low pay with the options
Worked on the engineers' backs until the 2004 listing
Cashed most of the options and retired
stories.payoff: Enough to retire on: in her own words a multi-multi-millionaire
stories.sting: She had only answered the advert on a whim, just divorced and living with her sister.
stories.note: There is no exact figure and none must be invented: the story is from the New York Times, 12 November 2007. A trade magazine gives the pay as $45 an hour for ten hours a week, the same $450.

stories.title_idea: How a Student Paid $35 for the Nike Logo Ended Up With 32,000 Shares
stories.payoff_figure: 500 Nike shares, which have since split into 32,000
stories.odd_means: was paid $35 for the logo, then handed shares twelve years later
stories.year_and_place: 1971 for the logo, September 1983 for the shares, Portland, Oregon
stories.terms: $35 for 17.5 hours of work
move: Drew a tick-shaped mark for a teacher's new shoe company
Billed $35
Twelve years on, was given a gold ring in the shape of the logo, with a diamond in it
And with it 500 shares
stories.payoff: The 500 shares have split into 32,000
stories.sting: She says she has never cashed in one of the original 500.
stories.note: Do not state a dollar value from memory: printed estimates run from $643,000 to $4 million depending on the date. Multiply 32,000 by the Nike price on the day. She has sold some of the split shares, only not the original 500.

stories.title_idea: How One Reply to a Tweet Made This Man a Billionaire
stories.hook_label: a man who answered a tweet
stories.odd_means: replied to a stranger's tweet with his email address
stories.terms: A founder tweeted that he wanted tips for a first hire at a start-up that had not launched
move: Saw the tweet
Replied the next day: here's a tip, email me
Became employee number one on 1 March 2010
Kept his shares to the 2019 listing
stories.payoff: About 2% of Uber at its listing: roughly $1.4 billion by Forbes's count
stories.sting: He was briefly made chief executive, then stepped aside for the man who had sent the tweet.
stories.who_real: Ryan Graves (public figure); the tweet was Travis Kalanick's
stories.note: Net worth is Forbes's running estimate ($1.4 billion and up, depending on the date).

stories.title_idea: How a Bookseller Sold Out of History's Biggest Bubble at the Top
stories.odd_means: sold his shares in the South Sea Bubble before it burst
stories.bigger_party: the South Sea Company and the crowd buying its shares
stories.terms: He had bought sailors' unpaid wage tickets at a deep discount, and in 1711 the government swapped them for South Sea shares
move: Bought seamen's pay tickets cheaply for decades
Had them turned into South Sea stock in 1711
Sold £54,040 of stock as the price soared in 1720
Moved the money into government annuities
stories.payoff: £234,428 for the lot: he multiplied his fortune about five times in a year
stories.sting: The next year he used it to found a hospital in London that still carries his name.
stories.who_real: Thomas Guy (died 1724; may be named), founder of Guy's Hospital
stories.note: His selling price per share is given as £600 by one source and an average of £420 by another: use only the £234,428 total. Know before posting: the South Sea Company traded in enslaved people, and his statue has been contested for it.

stories.title_idea: How a Rock Star Sold Shares in His Own Songs for $55 Million
stories.odd_means: sold bonds backed by ten years of his own royalties
stories.bigger_party: Prudential, the insurer that bought every bond
stories.terms: Ten-year bonds paying 7.9% a year, backed by the income from 25 albums
move: Pledged ten years of income from 25 albums
Sold the whole issue to one insurance company
Took $55 million in cash at once
stories.payoff: $55 million in hand, just before free music downloads arrived
stories.sting: By 2004 record sales had fallen so far that the bonds were cut to one notch above junk.
stories.note: The bonds were repaid in full on time. 'Downgraded to junk' (NPR) is loose: the 2004 rating, Baa3, is the lowest grade above junk. The first rating is given as Aaa by some and A3 by the Los Angeles Times: leave it out.

stories.title_idea: How This Woman Got Rich Heckling Bosses at Their Own Meetings
stories.hook_label: a woman who owned a few shares in everything
stories.payoff_figure: $600 a copy, two copies minimum, from the bosses of about 120 companies
stories.odd_means: heckled chief executives at their annual meetings, then sold them her newsletter
stories.year_and_place: 1965 to 2011, Washington and annual meetings across the USA
stories.terms: Owning even a few shares gave her the right to attend each company's annual meeting and take the microphone
move: Bought small holdings in about 120 big companies
Turned up at their meetings in a Batman mask, an aluminium dress, a swimsuit
Questioned the chief executive from the floor
Sold the same executives her yearly newsletter
stories.payoff: The newsletter reached $600 a copy with a two-copy minimum, and reportedly brought in $600,000 a year
stories.sting: Some of it stuck: companies including Macy's cut their directors' terms to one year, which she had demanded since 1988.
stories.who_real: Evelyn Y. Davis (died 2018; may be named)
stories.note: The $600,000 a year has ONE source (People magazine, 1996, quoted by Wikipedia); she herself claimed $250,000 in 1990. Always say 'reportedly'. The price and the two-copy rule are two-sourced. Critics said bosses subscribed to buy her goodwill: that is the argument.

stories.title_idea: How This Man Lives Almost Free on the Gifts Companies Send Shareholders
stories.hook_label: a retired board-game professional in Tokyo
stories.payoff_figure: a life paid for by vouchers: shares in over 1,000 companies, about 300 free cinema tickets a year
stories.odd_means: buys shares for the free gifts companies post to their shareholders
stories.terms: Many Japanese companies send their shareholders vouchers, called yutai: meals, cinema tickets, gym passes
move: Lost about 200 million yen in the 2008 crash
Got by on the vouchers he already had
Spread his money over more than 1,000 companies for their gifts
Cycles across Tokyo all day to use them before they expire
stories.payoff: Food, clothes, the gym and the cinema on vouchers: he says cash is for the rent and whatever vouchers will not cover
stories.sting: The bicycle he rides to use the vouchers was bought with vouchers.
stories.who_real: Hiroto Kiritani (living; a television personality in Japan)
stories.note: His own account, and the numbers differ by outlet (holdings from 100 million to 600 million yen; 500 to over 1,000 companies; the voucher habit dated to the 1989 or the 2008 crash). Keep to 'over 1,000 companies' and give no yen total for his wealth.

stories.title_idea: How a Dropout With Three Computers Won Nearly $1 Billion on Horses
stories.hook_label: a college dropout with three computers
stories.odd_means: wrote a computer model that priced horses better than the crowd did
stories.bigger_party: the Hong Kong Jockey Club's betting pools
stories.terms: A $150,000 stake, of which $120,000 was gone by the end of the first season
move: Flew to Hong Kong with three IBM computers
Fed years of race results into a model
Grew it to more than 120 factors for every horse
Bet wherever the crowd's odds were wrong
stories.payoff: Close to a billion dollars over the years by his own count, shared with partners
stories.sting: In 2001 his bets won a jackpot of about $16 million and he never collected it, so it went to charity.
stories.who_real: Bill Benter (living; public since a 2018 profile)
stories.note: A betting market, not shares, but it is a pricing story. 'Close to a billion' is his own estimate to Bloomberg Businessweek, the one primary source; the others repeat it.

stories.title_idea: How Eight Million Savers Were Handed Free Shares for Having a Bank Book
stories.payoff_figure: free shares worth more than £2,400 each on average: £18.4 billion in all
stories.odd_means: had a savings account or a mortgage with a building society on the day it became a bank
stories.bigger_party: the Halifax, Britain's biggest building society
stories.terms: A building society belongs to its savers and borrowers, so to join the stock market it had to pay them in shares
move: Kept an account open
Voted for the change
Received free shares in the post
Watched them open at 774.5p
stories.payoff: £18.4 billion of shares given away in a morning: one British adult in six was richer by more than £2,400 on average
stories.sting: People began opening accounts with £100 at other societies just to catch the next giveaway, and were named carpetbaggers.
stories.who_real: Halifax Building Society members (a group; no individual)
stories.note: A group with no single person, so the weakest fit to 'this man' among the 40. Member count is 7.6 million in one report and 'nearly eight million' in another. The £100 carpetbagger tactic is documented for societies in general, not for a named Halifax saver.

stories.title_idea: How a Professor and His Wife Turned $50,000 Into $750 Million
stories.hook_label: a chemistry professor and his wife
stories.odd_means: handed $25,000 each to a young family friend from Omaha and left it alone
stories.terms: $25,000 each into a small investment partnership run by a family friend
move: Gave the friend $25,000 each
Took shares in his company, Berkshire Hathaway, when the partnership closed
Never sold
Went on living quietly in Brooklyn
stories.payoff: His shares fetched about $210 million in 1995 and hers were valued at about $578 million in 1998
stories.sting: The friend was Warren Buffett, and almost all of it went to universities and a hospital.
stories.note: Total reported as $750 million to $800 million; the lower is used. Start date is 1961 in most accounts, 'early 1970s' in one. The fortune became public at their deaths: keep the reel on the holding.

stories.title_idea: How This Man Has Flown 23 Million Miles on One $290,000 Ticket
stories.hook_label: a car-dealership consultant from New Jersey
stories.odd_means: bought a lifetime pass that an airline sold and came to regret
stories.terms: $290,000 for unlimited flights for life
move: Flew, and kept flying: 373 flights in 2019 alone
Collected frequent-flyer miles on every one
stories.payoff: More than 23 million miles so far: he calls it the best investment of his life
stories.sting: In 2019 alone he flew 1.46 million miles on it.
stories.who_real: Tom Stuker (living; has given many interviews)
stories.note: A mispriced product, not a share story. One local report gives $510,000 for the pass; the Washington Post and the rest say $290,000.

stories.title_idea: How a $4 Flea-Market Painting Hid a $2.4 Million Piece of Paper
stories.hook_label: a man at a flea market
stories.odd_means: bought an ugly painting because he liked the frame
stories.bigger_party: the experts, who said $800,000 at most
stories.year_and_place: 1989, Adamstown, Pennsylvania; sold in New York on 13 June 1991
stories.terms: $4 for a torn painting in an old frame
move: Paid $4 for the frame
Took the painting out at home and found the frame could not be saved
Found a folded sheet hidden in the backing
Had it identified: a first printing of the Declaration of Independence, 4 July 1776
stories.payoff: $2.42 million at auction: three times the experts' top estimate
stories.sting: He sold too early: the same sheet went for $8.14 million in 2000.
stories.note: A price story (bought at $4, sold at $2.42 million), no shares. The number of surviving first printings is given as 24, 25 or 26: leave it out.

stories.title_idea: How a Scrap Dealer's Bad Deal Turned Out to Be a $33 Million Egg
stories.payoff_figure: an egg valued at about $33 million, bought for about $14,000
stories.odd_means: bought a gold ornament to melt down and could not find anyone to take it
stories.bigger_party: the antiques trade, which had lost it for a century
stories.year_and_place: bought in the American Midwest; identified in London in 2014
stories.terms: About $14,000 at a flea market, hoping to make $500 on the gold
move: Bought it for its weight in gold
Found no scrap buyer would pay what he had
Searched its markings online and found an article about lost eggs
Took it to a London dealer in Russian treasures
stories.payoff: It was the Third Imperial Easter Egg, made by Faberge for the Russian empress in 1887: valued at about $33 million
stories.sting: Nobody would buy it as scrap, and that is the only reason it was never melted.
stories.who_real: anonymous (never named); the dealer was Wartski of London
stories.note: $33 million is the dealer's valuation; the price the collector paid was never disclosed and one early report said $20 million. Say 'valued at', never 'sold for'.

stories.title_idea: How This Man Turned a $20 Web Address Into $2.6 Million
stories.hook_label: a 43-year-old who registered a web address
stories.odd_means: registered pizza.com in 1994 and kept paying the yearly fee
stories.bigger_party: the pizza chains that never bought it from him
stories.terms: $20 a year to hold the address
move: Registered pizza.com in 1994, hoping it would win his consulting firm a pizza client
Paid $20 a year to keep it
Heard that vodka.com had sold for $3 million
Put it up for a week-long online auction
stories.payoff: The bidding opened at $100 and a week later stood at $2.6 million
stories.sting: The winner bid anonymously and has never been named.
stories.note: Buying and selling, no shares. He paid about $280 in fees over the 14 years (14 x $20, my sum).

stories.title_idea: How a Student Made $1 Million Selling Dots on a Web Page
stories.odd_means: sold a million pixels of one web page at a dollar each
stories.terms: $1 a pixel, sold in blocks of 100: $100 minimum
move: Put up a page of a million blank pixels
Priced every one at $1
Let the newspapers do his advertising
Auctioned the last 1,000 on eBay
stories.payoff: Every pixel sold in about five months: $1,037,100 in all
stories.sting: The last 1,000 pixels went for $38,100: 38 times the list price.
stories.who_real: Alex Tew (living; now a known founder)
stories.note: A pricing tactic, no shares. The figure is gross sales, before costs and tax.

stories.title_idea: How This Gambler Haggled the Rules and Took $15 Million Off Three Casinos
stories.odd_means: bargained before he sat down: 20% of his losses back
stories.year_and_place: late 2010 to April 2011, Atlantic City, New Jersey
stories.terms: Casinos short of big players gave him 20% back on losses and rules that cut their edge to about a quarter of one percent
move: Negotiated the discount and the rules with each casino
Played for very high stakes
Won $5.8 million in one 12-hour sitting
stories.payoff: Nearly $6 million from the Tropicana, about $5 million from the Borgata and about $4 million from Caesars
stories.sting: He never counted a card: the casinos had bargained their own advantage away.
stories.note: RESERVE, not one of the 40: gambling, no market. A statistician writing in Chance magazine doubted the published rules alone explain the win.

stories.title_idea: How This Baseball Player Turned $5.9 Million Into $29.8 Million by Waiting
stories.hook_label: a baseball player his team no longer wanted
stories.odd_means: agreed to wait eleven years for his money at 8% interest
stories.terms: The team owed him $5.9 million and offered to pay it later, with 8% a year added
move: Was released in January 2000
Swapped the $5.9 million for 25 yearly payments starting in 2011
Waited
stories.payoff: $1,193,248.20 every 1 July from 2011 to 2035: $29.8 million
stories.sting: Fans now call 1 July by his name, and the club's new owner has talked of celebrating it at the stadium.
stories.note: RESERVE, not one of the 40: a pay deal, though the 8% rate is the whole story.

stories.title_idea: How This Man Traded One Red Paperclip Up to a House
stories.odd_means: swapped a paperclip for something slightly better, fourteen times
stories.bigger_party: nobody: every swapper thought they had the better deal
stories.terms: One red paperclip, offered online for something bigger or better
move: Posted the paperclip on Craigslist
Made 14 swaps in a year
Swapped the last item, a part in a film, with a small town for a farmhouse
stories.payoff: Fourteen trades turned a paperclip into a house in Kipling, Saskatchewan
stories.sting: The town put up a giant red paperclip in its park, at the time the largest in the world.
stories.who_real: Kyle MacDonald (living; wrote a book about it)
stories.note: RESERVE, not one of the 40: pure trading, but the payoff is a thing, not a sum.

stories.title_idea: How This Man Bought Google.com for $12
stories.odd_means: bought the address google.com when it showed up as for sale
stories.terms: $12 on Google's own shop for web addresses
move: Saw google.com listed as available
Paid $12 for it
Owned it for about a minute
Reported the hole to Google
stories.payoff: Google paid him $6,006.13: the word Google written in numbers
stories.sting: When he gave the reward to charity, Google doubled it.
stories.note: RESERVE, not one of the 40: fully sourced, small sum.

stories.title_idea: How a Dancer Made $2 Million in Shares by Telegram
stories.hook_label: a professional dancer on a world tour
stories.odd_means: sent his buy and sell orders by telegram from wherever he was dancing
stories.terms: A method of his own: buy a share when it breaks above its recent range
move: Read the share prices by cable each day
Wired orders to his broker
Sold when a share fell out of its range
stories.payoff: $2 million in about 18 months, he wrote; Time magazine gave him most of a page on 25 May 1959
stories.sting: His book sold so well that his method is still taught under his name.
stories.note: The $2 million rests on his own book; his starting money is given as $2,000, under $25,000 or $36,000. Not checked here: reports that New York's attorney general challenged the claims in 1960.

stories.title_idea: How a Pool Builder Sold His Car and Made Millions in Shares
stories.payoff_figure: $18 million from $10,775 (or $42 million, by another account)
stories.odd_means: sold his car to fund a share-trading account in the dot-com boom
stories.terms: About $11,000 from selling his car
move: Sold the car
Traded fast-rising technology shares full time
Sat through a 32% one-day fall in October 2000
stories.payoff: Profiled by Fortune on 18 December 2000 under the headline 'My Stocks Are Up 10,000%!'
stories.sting: At one point in the crash that followed his account was down 75%.
stories.note: The Fortune article could not be read; the sums ($18 million in 18 months, $42 million in 23 months) conflict across secondary sites.

stories.title_idea: How a Trader Turned Strangers From a Newspaper Advert Into Millionaires
stories.hook_label: a group of beginners hired through a newspaper advert
stories.payoff_figure: a claimed $175 million in five years
stories.odd_means: were taught one set of trading rules and given a rich man's money to trade
stories.terms: Adverts in the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times and Barron's drew about 1,000 applicants for 23 places
move: Answered the advert
Learned a fixed set of rules
Traded the founder's money by those rules
stories.payoff: The two classes are said to have earned more than $175 million
stories.sting: It began as a bet between two partners over whether trading can be taught.
stories.who_real: the 'Turtles' of Richard Dennis and William Eckhardt
stories.note: The $175 million comes from one former trainee and is given over four years or five; Nasdaq calls the story a legend with few hard facts.

stories.title_idea: How One Banker's Tip Filled a Small Town With Coca-Cola Millionaires
stories.hook_label: the people of a small farming town
stories.odd_means: bought Coca-Cola shares because the local banker told them to, and never sold
stories.bigger_party: Wall Street, which had given up on the share
stories.terms: The banker saw people spend their last coins on a Coke while the share sold for about the cash the company held
move: Took the banker's advice
Bought Coca-Cola shares
Held them through the Depression
Passed them down
stories.payoff: A town of a few thousand with dozens of Coca-Cola millionaires
stories.sting: Decades later about two-thirds of the local bank's trust assets were still in the one share.
stories.who_real: Pat Munroe of the Quincy State Bank, and his neighbours
stories.note: The count of millionaires is not established (25 in the state archive, 67 in the legend) and the trust-assets figure has one source.

stories.title_idea: How This Billionaire Kept His Fortune Through the Dot-Com Crash
stories.hook_label: a man paid entirely in another company's shares
stories.payoff_figure: a fortune of about $1.4 billion kept whole
stories.odd_means: bought insurance against his own shares falling, paid for by giving up the gains above a ceiling
stories.bigger_party: everyone who held on in the dot-com crash
stories.terms: Yahoo bought his company for $5.7 billion, all in Yahoo shares he could not sell at once
move: Bought the right to sell at $85
Sold someone else the right to buy at $205
Waited
stories.payoff: Yahoo's share price then fell by more than 90% and his stake held its value
stories.sting: He says he ended up with more than the sale first gave him.
stories.note: All of it traces to his own interviews; the option prices (85 and 205) and Yahoo's high and low differ between retellings.

stories.title_idea: How a Rapper Took Shares in a Drink and Made a Fortune
stories.odd_means: took a stake in the drinks company he advertised
stories.terms: A fee and a share of the company for fronting its vitamin drink
move: Agreed to advertise the drink
Took part of his pay as shares
Held until the company was sold
stories.payoff: Coca-Cola paid $4.1 billion in cash for the company on 25 May 2007
stories.sting: The company would never confirm how much of it he owned.
stories.note: Only the $4.1 billion sale is documented. His stake (5% to 10%) and payout ($100 million to a disputed $400 million) are unconfirmed, and he was reportedly paid a fee as well as shares.

stories.title_idea: How Two Lawyers Bought the Right to Bottle Coca-Cola for $1
stories.payoff_figure: the bottling rights for most of the United States
stories.odd_means: asked the owner for a right he thought was worthless
stories.terms: $1 for the exclusive right to bottle Coca-Cola across most of the country, with no end date
move: Asked for the bottling rights
Signed for $1
Sold local bottling licences to others across the country
stories.payoff: By the 1950s about 1,100 bottling businesses traced back to that contract
stories.sting: The company spent from the 1920s to 1986 buying the rights back.
stories.who_real: Benjamin Thomas and Joseph Whitehead (historical; may be named)
stories.note: No two-sourced figure for what the lawyers made, so the reel has no big number. 'He never collected the dollar' is an anecdote.

stories.title_idea: How an Economist Beat the Stock Market for 25 Years
stories.payoff_figure: about 8 percentage points a year ahead of the market for 25 years
stories.odd_means: put his college's money into shares when colleges held land and bonds
stories.terms: He ran the college's fund from 1921 until 1946
move: Moved the fund into company shares
Tried timing the market in the 1920s and did badly
Switched to buying a few shares and holding them
stories.payoff: His share portfolio beat the British market by an average of 8 points a year
stories.sting: In the fall of 1937 and 1938 he refused to sell, and resigned as chairman of an insurance company when its board would not follow him.
stories.who_real: John Maynard Keynes (died 1946; may be named)
stories.note: The gain is his college's, his own estate (about £400,000 in one report) is single-sourced, and 'he traded from his bed' is called a legend.

stories.title_idea: How Shoppers Got Two Flights to America for the Price of a Vacuum Cleaner
stories.hook_label: a few hundred thousand British shoppers
stories.odd_means: bought the cheapest vacuum cleaner that qualified, for the flights
stories.terms: Spend £100 on a Hoover product and get two free return flights, to America from November 1992
move: Bought a vacuum cleaner
Posted the form
Chased the company when the tickets did not come
stories.payoff: The flights cost Hoover about £50 million against some £30 million of sales
stories.sting: Only about 220,000 of the roughly half a million who applied are thought ever to have flown.
stories.note: Every number is an estimate (Hoover never published any) and most applicants did NOT come out ahead.

stories.title_idea: How Frequent Flyers Bought Money With Credit Cards and Flew Free
stories.payoff_figure: free air miles on up to $696,000 of spending each
stories.odd_means: bought dollar coins from the government on credit cards and paid them straight into the bank
stories.terms: The Mint sold $1 coins at face value and posted them free, to get the coins into use
move: Ordered boxes of coins on a card that pays air miles
Took delivery, post paid
Paid the coins into the bank
Cleared the card with the same money
stories.payoff: The Mint's 20 biggest customers each bought between $219,000 and $696,000 of coins
stories.sting: The Mint called it an abuse of the system and stopped taking credit cards in 2011.
stories.note: The buyers' figures come from one outlet (NPR) and no single person's gain is documented; a claim of 4 million miles has only a weak source.

stories.title_idea: How a $1,000 Share Purchase Became a 395-Acre Wildlife Sanctuary
stories.odd_means: bought shares in a chemist's chain on a tip and held them for about 70 years
stories.year_and_place: bought about 1950, given away in 2017, Chicago
stories.terms: About $1,000 of Walgreens shares
move: Bought $1,000 of shares
Held them for about seventy years
Gave the lot away while he was alive to see it
stories.payoff: About $2 million, given to the Illinois Audubon Society for a wildlife sanctuary
stories.sting: The sanctuary it paid for carries his name.
stories.note: The year he bought is 1947 or 1953 depending on the report; the sanctuary is 395 or 400 acres. The sums are two-sourced.

stories.title_idea: How a 12-Year-Old Won a Bet With His Parents Using Bitcoin
stories.payoff_figure: a million dollars by the age of 18
stories.odd_means: put a present from his grandmother into bitcoin
stories.bigger_party: his parents, who lost the bet
stories.terms: $1,000 from his grandmother, with bitcoin at about $12
move: Bought bitcoin with the $1,000
Bet his parents that a million by 18 would excuse him from university
Held
stories.payoff: He passed a million dollars in June 2017, aged 18, when bitcoin crossed $2,700
stories.sting: His parents kept their word: he never went.
stories.note: His holdings are his own word and the reports differ ($1,000 or $1,245; 83 or about 100 coins at first, 446 by 2019).
